claim: Practice-phase performance can run opposite to later retention: blocked or massed or restudy conditions win during learning, while random, spaced or tested conditions win on delayed tests.
agent_test: Compare a lesson or prompt change judged on its immediate pass rate versus a delayed, fresh-problem pass rate at equal tokens; count rank reversals.
audit_note: Numbers verified in 5 papers; minor: massed practice did not beat spaced during practice in Rohrer Exp1 (83 vs 82), and restudy won on a 5-min test rather than during learning.

claim: Learners misjudge this: in Kornell and Bjork 78% said massing was as good as or better than spacing even though 78% did better with spacing, in the replication 71% said massing produced most learning, and in Karpicke and Roediger predicted recall was flat at about 50% across conditions whose actual one-week recall ranged from about 33% to 80%.
agent_test: LLM analogue: ask the model to predict which of two scaffold variants will do better on a delayed test; compare its prediction with measured results.
audit_note: In Kornell and Bjork 78% said massing was as good as OR better (not preferred massing); Karpicke's flat predictions show insensitivity to condition, not a preference for the easier condition.
claim_before_audit: Learners misjudge this: they rate the easier, massed or blocked condition as better even when they performed worse on it (71-78% preferred massing in Kornell and Bjork and its replication; Karpicke predictions flat at about 50% across conditions).

claim: The spacing effect is reliable for verbal recall: optimal gap is about 20-40% of a 1-week delay and 5-10% of a 1-year delay; zero gap vs optimal gap gives d = 1.1 recall. Online replication (Rogers 2025) confirms spaced beats massed but the best-gap (lag) effect is mixed, so the ratio rule is not firm.
agent_test: Test a re-visit schedule for stored lessons (memory) at equal tokens: spaced re-checks versus all-at-once.
audit_note: Cepeda 2008 and Rogers 2025 verified; Rogers mostly found no lag effect (ANCOVA exception), so 'mixed' is a fair summary; two listed evidence lines (Kang, Rogers) merely repeat the claim text.

claim: Spacing benefit shrinks with task complexity: d = 0.97 for simple tasks, near 0.1 for complex tasks (Donovan and Radosevich), with mostly within-session massed-vs-spaced designs.
agent_test: Vary task difficulty class and check whether delay or interleaving of sub-steps still helps for hard problems.

claim: Testing beats restudy on delayed tests: pooled g about 0.50 in lab (Rowland), 0.499 in classrooms (Yang), 0.61-0.70 (Adesope), with high heterogeneity (I2 = 84%) and a reversal on immediate tests. Preregistered Higham 2023 (n=259) found restudy beat retrieval (0.74 vs 0.63-0.65) when a memory rating was required each trial.
agent_test: Retrieval from memory versus re-reading the lesson in context: compare delayed accuracy on matched problems at equal tokens.

claim: Testing effect transfers less well: d = 0.40 to new items overall, weakest to rearranged items and worked-example problems.
agent_test: Check that a lesson retrieved by test does not only help near-copies of the original problem; measure far-transfer problems.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Testing effect did not appear in an online Prolific replication-style test (null, F = 0.13, 40% attrition); boundary is sample and engagement, not clear refutation. Two further 2023 preregistered or Bayesian studies show reversals or nulls tied to rating/JOL steps (Higham: restudy 0.74 vs retrieval 0.65; Zhao: g=0.10, BF10=0.19).
agent_test: Not for agent; informs that human-subject nulls often come from low engagement.

claim: Unsuccessful retrieval attempts followed by feedback beat read-only study (d 0.38-1.49); errors of commission do not hurt.
agent_test: Let the agent attempt before being shown the answer or the failing output; compare with showing the solution first (G2 already shows feedback is needed).
audit_note: Kornell et al. 2009 numbers verified; second source is a Bjork review (shares coauthors) that reports the independent Huelser and Metcalfe 2012 wrong-guess result, so independence is thin but acceptable.

claim: Interleaving helps most when categories are similar to each other and exemplars within a category differ: full text of Brunmair and Richter confirms overall g = 0.42 [0.34, 0.50], paintings 0.67, photographs 0.35, maths 0.34, words -0.39, texts n.s.; similarity-between +0.22 and similarity-within -0.17 (Model 3); retention interval and retention-vs-transfer do not moderate; benefit is larger when items follow at once (g 0.73) than when spaced (0.22).
agent_test: Interleave problem types in the lesson memory versus blocking by type; test classification of new problems at equal tokens.
audit_note: All Brunmair and Richter numbers verified in full text (the three d-lines are the same paper); other listed sources (Kornell and Bjork, Rohrer and Taylor) support direction only; temporal-spacing g 0.22 is non-significant (CI -0.13 to 0.45).

claim: Interleaving effect holds in direct replications with identification and 2AFC tests (dz 0.43-0.48), but the replication authors say identification tests confound memory and response bias.
agent_test: Use a recognition-style test and an identification-style test of the agent's learned lessons and see if they agree.

claim: The interleaving classroom effect on high-stakes exams was null (d 0.02-0.20) when students crammed, though homework and surprise tests favoured interleaving.
agent_test: Check whether a delayed benefit survives when the test is set up with cramming (all lessons loaded in context).

claim: Generation and some other 'difficult' manipulations do not always help: text-generation effect found in 0 of 7 recall experiments and reversed in 4.
agent_test: Warns against assuming every added difficulty is desirable; test each by itself.

claim: Debiasing the illusion is hard: modest effects from instruction in 3 experiments; only seeing separated test results plus theory moved a majority.
agent_test: Show the tuning loop its own delayed-test results rather than telling it the principle; abstract only for b18.

claim: In-context blocked-vs-interleaved curriculum effects in LLMs mirror humans only partly: Llama 2 70B shows blocked better on a rule-like task (chi2 = 10.7, p = 0.001); GPT-3.5 does not reach significance in the supplement (p = 0.1). The test is immediate generalisation, not a delayed test. Abstract-only snippet (c26) says an interleaving effect also appears in GPT-4o-mini and Llama 3.1 in-context and is weaker in DeepSeek-V3; not opened in full. c06 and c07 are the same Russin paper (one source).
agent_test: In-context example order: blocked vs interleaved by rule-like versus rule-free tasks at equal tokens. Source counted once (three lines same paper).

claim: AI help that raises assisted performance can lower unassisted learning: GPT Base +0.137 practice (+48%) but -0.054 exam (-17%); GPT Tutor +0.361 (+127%) and -0.004 (null). Cross-check: Fan 2024 RCT (117 students) found ChatGPT raised essay score (F=4.549, eta2=0.108) with no knowledge-gain or transfer difference (F=0.913; F=0.019). Kosmyna 2025 (N=54, EEG) found LLM-first users under-engaged. Direction agrees (no learning benefit when the AI does the work); only Bastani shows actual harm (-17 percent). Measured in humans using an LLM, not in an LLM agent.
agent_test: Direct analogue of lesson judging: score memory lessons on unassisted held-out problems, not on assisted runs. b25 and b26 are conceptual or preprint support.
audit_note: Bastani and Fan numbers verified; Kosmyna not opened.

claim: Perceived-vs-actual learning gap occurs with AI tutors too: students rated GPT Tutor better despite null exam effect. Eleftheriou 2026 (85 participants): the standard LLM baseline gave high perceived understanding and the lowest objective learning; guided hints gave d=1.14, about +45 percent.
agent_test: b24 reports large immediate gains with no delayed test, so it cannot tell learning from performance.

claim: Replay of language-model training data by past difficulty beats uniform replay: TinyLlama old-Wikipedia accuracy uniform 25.2, perplexity-prioritised 27.4 (with the best new accuracy, 38.8), SM-2 interval scheduling 49.0 (new about 20.0). So priority by past failure helps on both axes, while interval scheduling buys retention at some plasticity cost. Weights are trained, not in-context. Full text re-checked this session: SRT old Wikipedia accuracy 49.0 vs uniform 25.2 vs PPL-prioritised 27.4, base 54.3, naive CPT 11.7; the abstract states 5 to 37 points of lost old-knowledge accuracy recovered. One paper, two model scales, recall signal borrowed from perplexity.
agent_test: Replay prioritised by past failure versus uniform replay of lessons; measure old and new accuracy. Neither study isolates a desirable-difficulty effect.

claim: Repeated data without spacing barely matters up to 4 epochs for pretraining loss; this is repetition and not a test of spacing. Muennighoff 2023: up to 4 epochs negligible loss change; decay constant R_D* about 15 repetitions (a learned decay constant, not a literal half-life). Xu 2026 extends with masked-input regularisation at 72M-1.4B.
agent_test: None direct; limits the analogy from human spacing to model training.

claim: Spaced-repetition models are practical: half-life regression cut recall-prediction error to 0.128 vs 0.235 for Leitner, but AUC about 0.5 and A/B outcomes measure engagement.
agent_test: If lesson memory has a decay model, compare against a plain recency rule for which lessons to surface.

claim: Difficulty must match learner expertise and material complexity; desirable difficulty can become undesirable for low-skill or complex-task learners. LLM analogues: constrained prompts help gpt-4o (97 vs 93) but not gpt-5 (94.00 vs 96.36 on full GSM8K, one researcher); scaffolds help weak receivers and can turn negative (51 of 59 predicted signs). Pass 2: a year-long field RCT finds interleaving gains short-term (+0.28 SD) but not on the cumulative test, concentrated in lower achievers; self-reflection helps most when initial correctness is low (Li 2024); explicit CoT lowers instruction following across 15 models.
agent_test: S0 gate: apply extra difficulty only to classes with a high plain pass rate; test on easy versus hard classes.

claim: Distributed placement of repeated material inside an LLM context improves retention of a Markov-chain task over massed or single exposure, with a sweet spot at intervals of 100-400 steps (1-4 segment lengths); gradient-based continual learning shows no such spot. Janik 2024 (figure-only, qualitative) agrees: repetition after a separation raises recall over a single exposure, permuted slightly better than verbatim; related distractor lists hurt most. Small and synthetic tasks.
agent_test: Re-show a stored lesson after 1, 2, 4, 8 intervening tasks versus back-to-back; score on held-out problems at equal tokens.
audit_note: Kang and Janik verified; both are small synthetic/preprint LLM studies as the claim notes.

claim: Self-authored agent skills do not help and can hurt: -8.1 to -11.5 pp against no skills, while curated skills add +18.2 to +24.8 pp (87 tasks, three harnesses). Abstraction memory also trails raw-trajectory memory on held-out tasks (49.0 vs 53.5 percent over nine settings). Caveat from the SkillsBench authors: the self-generated deficit mixes content quality with skill-discovery and creator-solver interference. The SkillsBench abstract now reports curated gain +16.6 pp over 18 configurations (33.9 to 50.5); the +18.2 to +24.8 pp figures are the three dedicated harnesses.
agent_test: Score every new lesson by held-out pass rate with and without it; never by the run that wrote it.
audit_note: SkillsBench and Wang et al. numbers verified including the caveat; the d08/d09 lines merely repeat the claim text.

claim: Easy-to-hard ordering of in-context demonstrations beats random order on instruction-tuned LLMs (about +9 percent average) and hurts base models (-7.16 percent); the test is immediate.
agent_test: Order lesson examples easy-to-hard versus hard-first, then re-test after unrelated tasks.

claim: No study found tests attempt-before-lesson versus lesson-first for an LLM at equal tokens; the only attempt-first result with an AI tool is human (N = 61, reported d = 8.59 that does not match its own means). Pass 2: a second human study (Struggle First, n=60, final test d=1.54 for attempt-first, same week) and the ExpRAG finding that stored failed attempts still help; still no LLM test at equal tokens.
agent_test: Run it: agent attempts the problem and sees its failure, then the lesson, versus lesson first; same tokens; delayed held-out set.

claim: Verbalised LLM confidence is a weak signal of capability on an item once consensus items are removed (20 models, 6 benchmarks); no study found asks an LLM which of two schemas will do better on a delayed test. Huff and Ulakci 2024: human judgments of learning predicted later memory (B=0.104, CI 0.005 to 0.202, N=78); GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4o did not (CIs include zero). Scope: LLM judgments of human memory and verbalised confidence; neither tests an LLM predicting its own delayed gain from a schema. Pass 2: verbalised confidence is overoptimistic across 12 LLMs and 38 tasks, with effort appraisals matching or beating it; prompt-quality predictors do not transfer (snippet level). Still no direct pairwise-schema test.
agent_test: Ask the model to rank two schema variants, then measure them; count how often the model prefers the easier variant.
audit_note: Moran/Whiting, Huff/Ulakci and Beyond Confidence verified; the 'prompt-quality predictors do not transfer' clause and the no-direct-study negative were not checked.

claim: The spacing effect holds in a large online replication (162 analysed) but the best-gap effect is inconsistent across analyses; exact ratio rules should not be hard-coded.
agent_test: Sweep the revisit gap on the agent and pick it empirically.

claim: Interleaving should help ARC-like classes (similar transform types, varied exemplars) more than word-like or text-like brainteasers, by the Brunmair moderators; this is a prediction not yet measured on LLMs, and blocked order wins when a rule can be read from a block.
agent_test: Per problem class, compare blocked and interleaved lesson order on a delayed held-out set.

claim: Replay scheduled by spaced-repetition state (SM-2 with per-example perplexity as the recall signal) restores old knowledge far better than uniform replay at the same 20/80 replay budget: TinyLlama old accuracy 49.0 vs 25.2 (base 54.3, naive continual pre-training 11.7); Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct 51.6 vs 46.2 (base 50.2). It stays near base on MMLU, BBH, GSM8K where uniform replay collapses BBH to 8.4 and GSM8K to 6.8. Cost: new-knowledge accuracy about 20.0 vs 38.8 for the perplexity-prioritised variant.
agent_test: Give a lesson memory a revisit schedule (SM-2-like state per lesson) vs uniform vs most-failed-first retrieval at equal tokens; score old-task and new-task pass rates.

claim: Inside one coherent domain at fixed data volume, blocked vs interleaved vs order effects in LLM fine-tuning are mostly inside run-to-run noise (average 0.010-0.021 against a 0.019 floor over 761 runs, 12 base models); the largest contrast, 0.0619, read +0.010 and -0.015 on two reruns. Scored on the capability both skills were trained for, interleaving does beat blocking (+0.0483, 6 of 6 pairs), and 76 percent of that is less forgetting of the skill trained first.
agent_test: When comparing two lesson orders or two schemas, rerun about 4 times per arm and report the floor; score on all trained skills, not the last one.

claim: Order effects flip with conditions: when the pooled corpus holds conflicting but equally correct answer conventions, arrangement matters a lot (allocation moves -0.268 and -0.443 vs -0.005 control; Qwen3-8B -0.0875, 5 of 5 seeds negative), and writing the convention into the input switches this off.
agent_test: Tag every stored lesson with the conditions under which it holds, and test whether tagged lessons remove order sensitivity.

claim: Easy-to-hard or difficulty-ordered curricula give inconsistent LLM gains: 200+ pretraining models reach baseline with 18-45 percent fewer steps and up to 3.5 percent sustained gain, depending on the difficulty metric (Zhang 2026); a study across Llama, Qwen and Gemma sizes found no robust gain over random sampling (Mordig 2026); Elgaar 2026 finds partial effects; in-context easy-to-hard demonstration order gives about +9 percent on instruction-tuned and -7.16 percent on base models (Liu 2024).
agent_test: Order stored lessons or in-context demonstrations easy-to-hard vs random vs hard-first at equal tokens, on an instruction-tuned model, and read the delta against the run-to-run floor.

claim: LLM knowledge absorption in weight training depends on varied or self-generated study forms, not on verbatim repetition: without augmentation extraction accuracy is near 0 percent even when facts are seen (Allen-Zhu and Li); models that paraphrase, self-quiz and associate a document before training reach 66 percent on a Wikipedia SimpleQA subset vs 7.42 for the base 8B model (+313 percent relative over vanilla fine-tuning, Lin 2025). This is an analogue of elaboration and retrieval practice, not a test of delayed-after-harder-practice.
agent_test: Before storing a lesson, have the agent restate it, quiz itself on it, and link it to two older lessons; compare held-out transfer vs storing the lesson verbatim at equal tokens.
audit_note: Allen-Zhu and Li and Lin et al. verified; note 'depends on ... not verbatim repetition' is an interpretation, and Lin's 7.42 is the base model while +313% is relative to vanilla fine-tuning, as the claim states.

claim: Guardrailed AI help (hints and not answers, guided hints, contrast) avoids the learning loss that unrestricted help causes: Bastani GPT Tutor exam -0.004 (null) vs GPT Base -0.054; Eleftheriou 2026 guided hints d=1.14 and about +45 percent vs baseline with workload unchanged, while the contrastive design had the highest mental demand and a non-significant effect (d=0.74, p=0.080). Kestin 2025 reports AI tutoring beating in-class active learning (median 4.5 vs 3.5) but with no delayed test.
agent_test: Compare a hint-first scaffold step (agent gets a hint from its own memory, not the solved answer) against answer-first at equal tokens on a delayed held-out set.

claim: The central desirable-difficulties claim (harder practice looks worse now, better later) is untested for LLM agents: no study in evidence a-d scores a delayed, held-out test after harder vs easier practice. Closest proxies are Chen interleaving (fine-tuning), Kang spacing (in-context), SRT replay (weights) and Bastani (humans using an LLM). Pass 2 found nearer proxies (held-out agent-memory studies d18, d19, d21) but none compares harder vs easier lesson conditions; the gap stays open.
agent_test: Run the missing experiment: lessons learned under easy vs hard (interleaved, attempt-first) conditions, scored on a held-out set after a gap of N unrelated tasks.

claim: Search-selected winners in order or recipe space do not survive reruns: a pair fixed in advance resolves 0.031, a pair picked by search resolves 0.144, and 2 of 6 pairs reverse sign between independent runs. A gain seen once is a poor selection signal, in line with the human finding that practice-phase gain misleads. Independent support: single-run pass@1 spreads 2.2-6.0 pp with SD above 1.5 pp at temperature 0 (60,000 SWE-Bench trajectories), and the best strategy wins only 77% of head-to-head runs (ReasonBENCH, 30 trials).
agent_test: Before keeping a schema change, rerun it; accept only if the gain exceeds the measured floor of the same schema rerun with new seeds.

claim: Aggregate seen-versus-held-out gap for stored lessons: tips extracted from trajectories give larger gains on tasks they were built from than on held-out tasks (AppWorld, GPT-4.1: dev +12.3 pp task goal completion vs held-out +3.6; scenario goal +26.3 vs +14.3). Judging a lesson on its source tasks overstates its transfer. No per-lesson correlation exists.
agent_test: Log each lesson's pass rate on its source task and its gain on held-out tasks; compute a per-lesson rank correlation over at least 30 lessons.

claim: Lesson stores degrade when rewritten: consolidating lessons incrementally is the worst schedule on the same pool; GPT-5.4 failed 54% of ARC-AGI problems it solved without memory after consolidating; episodic-only memory matches or beats forced consolidation (about 2x); per-task fresh consolidation beat cumulative by 203 ScienceWorld points. Proposed mechanism: applicability conditions are stripped.
agent_test: Keep raw episodes; store each lesson with its trigger condition; compare consolidate-every-time vs consolidate-on-demand on held-out tasks.

claim: In a clean in-context episode store, retention policies are not separable at 50 held-out tasks: success-scored 49/50 and 48/50, FIFO 48/50, unbounded 47/50, no memory 39/50, with overlapping Wilson CIs; scoring only helps under 75% distractor writes. So the revisit-schedule question (gap 4) cannot be answered from this work.
agent_test: Test SM-2-like revisit vs most-failed-first vs uniform on at least 200 held-out tasks with paired reruns.

claim: Run-to-run noise is large enough to hide small schema effects: single-run pass@1 spreads 2.2-6.0 pp (SD above 1.5 pp at temperature 0, 60,000 SWE-Bench-Verified trajectories); the best reasoning strategy wins only 77% of head-to-head runs against its nearest competitor over 30 trials. Trajectories diverge within the first few percent of tokens. Bjarnason et al. estimate about 9 runs per agent to detect a 2 pp gain and about 36 for 1 pp, so a few seeds are not enough for small effects.
agent_test: Measure the SD of our own agent across at least 5 reruns at equal tokens before comparing schemas; use paired per-item tests.
audit_note: Noise numbers verified, but the '3 seeds floor, 5 or more for strong claims' is not in either source; Bjarnason et al. say detecting a 2 pp gain needs about 9 runs and a 1 pp gain about 36.
claim_before_audit: Run-to-run noise is large enough to hide small schema effects: single-run pass@1 spreads 2.2-6.0 pp (SD above 1.5 pp at temperature 0, 60,000 SWE-Bench-Verified trajectories); the best reasoning strategy wins only 77% of head-to-head runs over 30 trials. A practitioner floor is 3 seeds, 5 or more for strong claims. Trajectories diverge within the first few percent of tokens.

claim: Interleaving in a year-long field RCT (Nigerian primary schools, NBER w31853): +0.28 SD on short-term tests, no average effect on the cumulative end-of-year test, gains concentrated in lower achievers and little or none for high achievers. Not a null on the lab effect, but a limit on how long and for whom it holds.
agent_test: Score lesson-order effects on a cumulative end-of-run test, and split by baseline pass rate.

claim: Attempt-first with an AI helper (humans): students who attempted a problem before ChatGPT scored 91.85 vs 78.59 on the final test (n=60, d=1.54, same-week test); AI-guided vs fixed pretesting did not differ (85.71 vs 83.56, p=.319); a harder task favoured AI-guided pretesting (76.87 vs 69.65, p=.018). Task complexity as moderator is suggested, not tested.
agent_test: Compare attempt-first and lesson-first for the agent on simple vs complex item classes.
